- Global test: Pearson χ² = 75.20, df = 18; Monte-Carlo permutation p = 0.0002 (10,000 permutations, habitat margins fixed — used instead of the asymptotic test because 4 habitats have ≤8 records). Pathway composition differs strongly across habitats.
- Per-habitat Fisher exact tests (gardening vs all others) all significant after BH correction (largest q = 1.08e-06, Rock outcrops), but the four sparse habitats (≤8 records: Rock outcrops, Broad-leaved, Scrublands, Coniferous) are flagged as unstable — not collapsed, per your instruction.
- Firth logistic (share of gardening among records ~ habitat, ref = Croplands; Firth used because plain IRLS diverged under complete separation — Broad-leaved 4/4, Rock outcrops 0/1): Croplands logit −1.48 (share 0.19); all habitats trend toward higher gardening shares than Croplands, but only Wetlands (OR 2.09, CI [1.00,4.35]) borders significance vs Croplands; Coastal OR 1.98 [0.91,4.34]. The Wilson CIs above are the more informative uncertainty statement at this sample size.

== SECONDARY: plot-level intensity (632 plots; 191 invaded, 441 all-zero) ==
- With habitat as the only predictor, the per-plot binomial model on n.gard/(n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo) reduces exactly to the habitat-aggregated fit (sufficient statistics), so the coefficients above double as the plot-level share model. Dispersion diagnostic: observed variance of habitat shares is 8.8× the binomial expectation — habitat effects are real, not binomial noise; a beta-binomial would widen CIs modestly but not change the ranking. I did NOT add a zero-inflated model, per your guardrail (no identifiability-risk over-engineering).
- Distinct two-part piece added — probability a plot contains ≥1 gardening species (all 632 plots, Firth logistic, ref = Croplands): presence rates Wetlands 0.50 (19/38), Urban 0.48 (31/65), Coastal 0.45 (13/29), Riparian 0.36 (22/61), Croplands 0.21, Meadows 0.08, Coniferous 0.06, Broad-leaved 0.04, Scrublands 0.02, Rock outcrops 0.00. Odds ratios vs Croplands: Wetlands 1.77, Urban 1.71, Coastal 1.58, Riparian 1.35 — all CIs include 1 (moderate n), but the direction is consistent.
- Gardening records per plot: Coastal 0.79, Wetlands 0.76, Urban 0.69, Riparian 0.57, Croplands 0.22, Meadows 0.10, Coniferous 0.09, Broad-leaved 0.06, Scrublands 0.02, Rock outcrops 0.00. Total non-native records/plot: Urban 2.32, Riparian 1.57, Coastal 1.48, Wetlands 1.37 vs ≤0.33 elsewhere.

== Where the two prevalence views diverge ==
Share view: gardening dominates the composition of the non-native flora in wetlands (56%), coastal (53%) and forested plots (88–100%, sparse), while croplands (19%) and urban plots (30%) are dominated by unintentionally introduced species. Density view: gardening species are most frequent per plot in urban (0.69), coastal (0.79), wetland (0.76) and riparian (0.57) plots — urban has the highest overall invasion pressure (2.32 records/plot), so gardening is common there in absolute terms even though it is a minority share of its non-native flora. Forested/scrubland/rock habitats have few non-natives at all (0.02–0.10 records/plot), so their high gardening *shares* rest on very few records.

== Supporting context (not needed for the habitat answer) ==
- Species-level: 42/81 taxa are gardening-introduced; gardening taxa have median 2 invaded plots vs 3 for unintentional taxa.
- Temporal table, one line: gardening introductions rose from 18 species (pre-1500) to 397 (1985–2019), the dominant recent pathway region-wide.
- Phylogeny kept as supporting context only: all 81 taxa match the tree's 81 leaves (no phylogenetic signal analysis run, per guardrail 3).

== DRAFT NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS ==
"Non-native plants introduced via gardening are a markedly larger share of the invaded non-native flora in wet, coastal and forested habitats than in croplands: gardening accounts for ~56% of non-native species records in wetlands (29/52; 95% CI 42–68%), ~53% in coastal habitats (23/43; 39–67%) and ~88–100% in coniferous/broad-leaved forest plots (but only 8 and 4 records, respectively — unstable), versus only ~19% in croplands (20/108; 12–27%) and ~30% in urban plots (45/151; 23–38%), where unintentionally introduced species dominate (χ²=75.2, df=18, permutation p=0.0002). In absolute per-plot terms the picture partially diverges: gardening-introduced species are most frequent in urban, coastal, wetland and riparian plots (0.6–0.8 records/plot; present in 36–50% of plots) because these habitats are the most heavily invaded overall (1.4–2.3 non-native records/plot), whereas croplands, despite moderate invasion, are dominated by unintentional introductions. Thus, the relative importance of the gardening pathway is highest in wetlands, coastal sites and forests, while its absolute contribution peaks in human-disturbed, mesic habitats (urban, coastal, riparian, wetlands); estimates for rock outcrops, scrublands and both forest types rest on ≤8 records and should be treated with caution."

payload.workflow: Firth-penalized logistic GLMs (habitat factor, ref=Croplands) on (1) gardening share of 481 invaded-species records per habitat, (2) gardening presence across all 632 plots; Monte-Carlo permutation chi-square (10,000 perms, habitat margins fixed) for pathway x habitat association; per-habitat Wilson CIs and Fisher exact tests with BH correction; overdispersion diagnostic; sparse habitats (<=8 records) flagged, not collapsed; phylogeny used only to confirm tip-taxon match (81/81); temporal trends mentioned as one-line context.
